Two identical scoops of ice cream are taken from a refrigerator and put into paper cup X and vacuum flask Y. At room temperature they melt completely in times tX and tY. Which result and explanation are correct?

A. tX > tY, as the vacuum flask reduces heat loss to the surroundings.

B. tX > tY, as the vacuum flask retains heat.

C. tY > tX, as the vacuum flask keeps things cold by releasing heat.

D. tY > tX, as the vacuum flask reduces the rate of heat gain from the surroundings.

The surroundings are warmer than the ice cream, so net heat flows into it. Melting requires latent heat.

Insulation slows heat gain, so the identical scoop in Y takes longer: tY > tX. Choose D. A vacuum flask does not actively cool its contents by releasing heat.

2014|paper-1a|10.question:
* A particle is projected horizontally towards a vertical wall 1.0 m away. It hits the wall 0.8 m below its projection point. Find its initial speed. Neglect air resistance; g = 9.81 m s−2.

Horizontal velocity stays constant, so u = 1.0/t = 2.48 m s−1 ≈ 2.5 m s−1: B. Use the vertical drop to obtain the flight time first.

2014|paper-1a|11.question:
* An astronaut in a spacecraft moving in a circular orbit around the Earth is apparently weightless because

A. the astronaut is too far away to feel the Earth's gravitational force.

B. the astronaut and spacecraft have the same acceleration towards the Earth.

C. the Earth's gravitational force on the astronaut is balanced by the floor reaction.

D. the Earth's gravitational force on the astronaut is balanced by the centripetal force.

The astronaut and spacecraft are both in free fall, accelerating towards the Earth together. No supporting normal force is needed, so the apparent weight is zero: B.

Gravity is still present and supplies the centripetal force. Centripetal force is the name of the inward resultant, not an extra force balancing gravity.

2014|paper-1a|12.question:
* A satellite moves in a circular orbit at a height above the Earth equal to the Earth's radius. Find its acceleration in terms of the surface gravitational acceleration g.

B. g/4

C. g/2

D. g

a = GM/(2R)² = ¼GM/R² = g/4: B. Gravitational acceleration varies inversely as the square of distance from the centre.

A transverse wave travels left along a long string. Which statements correctly describe the motions of particles P, Q, R and S at the instant shown?

R crosses the equilibrium line on a steep slope and is not at rest. For this sinusoidal travelling wave, rest occurs at crests and troughs, not zero displacement. Only (1) is correct: A.

2014|paper-1a|15.question:
The figure shows a light ray travelling from medium I to medium III through parallel boundaries. Arrange the light speeds in ascending order.

2014|paper-1a|16.question:
Plane sea waves pass through a gap in a sea wall and diffract. Assuming frequency remains unchanged, which changes increase diffraction?

Diffraction becomes more pronounced when the wavelength-to-gap-width ratio λ/a increases. A narrower gap or a longer wavelength increases this ratio.

2014|paper-1a|17.question:
A car moves at uniform speed away from a stationary ultrasound generator and detector at Y. A pulse is emitted when the car is 64 m from Y. The emitted and reflected pulses appear on the CRO as shown. Estimate the car speed. The ultrasound speed in air is 340 m s−1.

The reflection point is 340(0.20) = 68 m from Y. During those 0.20 s the car travels 68−64 = 4 m, giving v = 4/0.20 = 20 m s−1: B. Do not use 0.50 s as the elapsed time.

Loudspeakers S1 and S2 are connected to a signal generator but produce sound in anti-phase. O is equidistant from them. S1P = 2.8 m and S2P = 3.0 m. With wavelength 10 cm, what interference occurs at O and P respectively?

The sources start π radians out of phase. At O the path difference is zero, so the waves remain in anti-phase and interfere destructively.

At P, Δr = 3.0−2.8 = 0.20 m = 2λ. This adds 4π phase difference, leaving the original anti-phase relation unchanged. P is also destructive: C. Integer-wavelength path difference only means constructive interference for in-phase sources.

An insulated solid X is heated at constant power. The graph shows temperature against time. Its specific heat capacity in the solid state is 800 J kg−1 °C−1. Find its specific latent heat of fusion.

Two insulated uncharged metal spheres X and Y touch. A positive rod is brought near X. X is touched momentarily by a finger, then Y is moved away to separate the spheres. The rod is removed afterwards. What are the final charges on X and Y respectively?

2014|paper-1a|21.question:
Three point charges Q1, Q2, Q3 lie on a straight line with Q2 at the midpoint. The resultant electrostatic force on each is zero. Which signed charges, in the same arbitrary units, are possible? Options list Q1, Q2, Q3.

2014|paper-1a|25.question:
Bulbs P and Q are connected to a 6 V cell of negligible internal resistance. The voltmeter reads 6 V when S is closed. Which is possible?

2014|paper-1a|27.question:
A long straight wire MN and rectangular coil PQRS are fixed in the same plane. Current I is positive from M to N and varies with time as shown. What is the induced-current direction in the coil during 0 to T?

2014|paper-1a|28.question:
A closely packed long solenoid has cross-sectional area A, length L and N turns, carrying a constant direct current. Which change increases the magnetic flux density at its central cross-section? Options list length, area and total turns.

2014|paper-1a|29.question:
* Current flows from right to left in a metal block with cross-section PQRS. With a uniform magnetic field applied, side PQ has higher electric potential than side SR. Which field direction is possible?

* A radium nucleus decays to a radon nucleus and an α-particle, releasing 4.9 MeV. Compared with the mass of the radium nucleus, the total mass of the radon nucleus and α-particle is

Two light strings pass over smooth pegs at the same height and support a weight W. Their other ends carry weights 30 N and 20 N. The system is in equilibrium, with the angles θ and φ shown. Which deduction is correct?

2014|paper-1a|5.question:
A particle moves along a straight line with uniform acceleration. It takes 4 s to travel 36 m, then 2 s to travel the next 36 m. What is its acceleration?

2014|paper-1a|6.question:
Two identical small blocks slide from rest down smooth inclined planes from the same height H. Their speeds at the bottom are v1, v2 and travel times are t1, t2. Neglect air resistance. Which is correct?

Conservation of mechanical energy gives mgH = ½mv², so both bottom speeds are √(2gH).

Along a plane inclined at θ, a = g sin θ and t = v/a. Plane (1) is steeper, so its acceleration is larger and its time shorter. Therefore v1 = v2, t1 < t2: D.

2014|paper-1a|7.question:
Sphere P of mass 2 kg collides head-on with sphere Q of mass 1 kg, initially at rest. P has speed 6 m s−1 just before collision. Both move in the same direction after collision. Which could be the speed(s) of Q just after collision?

D. (1), (2) and (3)

At the end of collision Q must not be slower than P behind it, otherwise they would still be approaching. The 2 m s−1 case fails this condition. The 4 and 6 m s−1 cases permit common motion or separation, and both reduce kinetic energy. Choose C.

2014|paper-1a|8.question:
Blocks of masses 5 kg and 3 kg are joined by a light string over a frictionless fixed light pulley. Find their acceleration magnitude when released, in terms of g. Neglect air resistance.

Add the equations: (5−3)g = (5+3)a, hence a = g/4: C. The driving force is the weight difference, but the accelerated mass is the sum.

2014|paper-1a|9.question:
A particle is projected vertically downwards from a rooftop at 2.0 m s−1 and reaches the ground at 11 m s−1. Estimate the height. Neglect air resistance; g = 9.81 m s−2.

h = (11²−2.0²)/(2×9.81) = 5.96 m ≈ 6.0 m: B. Subtract the initial speed squared, not the speed itself.

(a) 5 min, or 300 s. [1A]

(b) At switch-off the heater is hotter than the metal; heat continues to conduct to the metal until their temperatures become equal. [1A]

(c)(i) mcΔT = IVt. [1M]

0.80c(45−20) = 4.0×12×(5×60), so c = 720 J kg−1 °C−1. [1A]

(c)(ii) This calculation attributes all electrical energy to the metal. Since some energy goes elsewhere, the numerator is too large for the observed metal temperature rise and c is overestimated.

(a) The source is sealed in a thin metal casing. Explain why the NASA worker shown handling the RTG with bare hands need not be concerned about the emitted α particles. (1 mark)

*(b)(i) Calculate the activity at launch, in Bq. (3 marks)

(b)(ii) Each decay releases 5.5 MeV. Calculate the source’s power at launch, in kW. (2 marks)

(b)(i) k = ln 2 / t1/2 = ln 2 /(87.74×3.16×107) ≈ 2.5×10−10 s−1. [1M]

A = kN = [ln 2 /(87.74×3.16×107)]×3.2×1025. [1M] A = 8.000×1015 Bq. [1A]

(b)(ii) P = energy per decay × activity = 5.5×106×1.60×10−19×8.000×1015. [1M] P = 7040 W = 7.040 kW. [1A]

(b)(iii) P ∝ A ∝ N, so the percentage left is (1/2)36/87.74×100%. [1M] This is 75.25% ≈ 75%, or about three quarters. [1A] Alternatively use e−(ln 2/87.74)×36×100%.

(b)(i), accepted alternative unit: k = 7.9×10−3 year−1. Convert to s−1 before calculating activity in Bq.

(b)(i) Bq means decays per second, so convert the half-life to seconds before finding k. Multiply k by the number of undecayed atoms, not by their mass.

(b)(ii) First convert MeV per decay into joules per decay: 5.5 MeV = 8.8×10−13 J. Multiplying by decays per second gives joules per second. The 7.04 kW is radioactive thermal power, not the RTG’s electrical output; no conversion efficiency is given.
